blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Use precise, graded evaluative vocabulary; give a balanced verdict the reader can act on.

blocks.heading: Evaluative lexis
blocks.text: Evaluative lexis is the vocabulary of judgement: graded words that say how good, how bad, and in what way, rather than the general praise that could attach to anything. Graded vocabulary runs from the adequate to the outstanding and from the disappointing to the dire, and the grade names the level — a review that only says "good" and "bad" has a scale with two rungs, and a reader climbing it learns almost nothing.

blocks.heading: The balanced verdict
blocks.text: A balanced verdict is a weighed judgement: it names the best and the worst, and says which the reader should weight — for whom the thing is worth it, and for whom it is not. A list of likes and dislikes is a tally, and a tally is not a judgement: the reader of a tally must do the weighing themselves, which is the job they came to the review to have done. The verdict’s last sentences are its terms: who should come, who should not, and why.

blocks.heading: Taste without an argument
blocks.text: Offering personal likes and dislikes with no criteria and no critique is taste without an argument: the reader learns what the reviewer enjoyed and nothing about whether they would enjoy it. "I loved the music, I hated the queue" is a diary; "the music was the evening’s best half-hour — a five-piece band playing to the room rather than the stage — and the queue for it was badly managed, one door for three hundred tickets" is a review, because the criteria are in the sentences and the reader can weigh them. The cure is the same at every level: criteria first, evidence with them, and the verdict earned rather than asserted.

blocks.heading: Worked example: grading the lexis
blocks.text: Watch the grades do their work in one sentence: "The set was outstanding — a two-storey invention the audience kept discovering — the second act dragged to adequate, and the third rescued the evening from the second." "Outstanding" names the top rung; "adequate" names the middling one, and the drop is the judgement; "rescued" is evaluative lexis doing narrative work, because the evening’s shape is part of its worth. A reader holding this sentence knows what to pay for, what to endure, and in which order — which is the whole review, compressed.

blocks.heading: In the exam
blocks.text: The review question is one of the three Section B categories, set as a review in every paper of the corpus — 600–900 words, twenty-five marks, the same five strands as the rest of Section B. The reader the brief names is the review’s audience: a website’s browsers, a magazine’s subscribers, and the register and the criteria are chosen for them. Plan the five — context, thing, criteria, evidence, verdict — write the evaluation three times the length of the account, grade every judgement with the ladder this section teaches, and end on terms the reader can act on, which is the last service a review owes and the one its reader came for.
